report.releaseDate: Oct 2026 (NGB Annual Report 2025/26 tabled; MTBPS 21 Oct 2026; audited FY2024/25 statistics published 2 Oct 2025 / Apr 2026)
report.currency: ZAR (South African rand), tables in billions unless stated; ~USD alongside at USD/ZAR 16.6
report.verdict: South Africa is now a R84.5bn (~$5.1bn) GGR market whose growth is entirely online bookmaking: betting is 70% of GGR, ~86% of it online, and the land-based estate is shrinking. The rules are moving against the online channel — a proposed 20% national tax on online GGR (decision Feb 2027), new advertising norms, and an NGB site-blocking programme — while interactive casino remains illegal and licensing stays provincial. For B2Tech the prize is real but the licence-to-tax arbitrage that built the market is closing.

kpis.label: Online share of all GGR (NGB est.)

summary: **Market size: R84.46bn (~$5.09bn) GGR in FY2025/26 (1 Apr 2025–31 Mar 2026), +13.4% on the audited FY2024/25 figure of R74.50bn (~$4.49bn).** Turnover (stakes, including recycled winnings) reached ~R1.76tn (~$106bn) vs R1.50tn (~$90bn). FY2025/26 figures come from the NGB Annual Report tabled in October 2026 as relayed by The Citizen/Focus Gaming News; Gauteng's contribution is flagged as provisional and unaudited.

**Growth is decelerating but still double-digit.** Audited GGR grew 36.9% (FY21/22), 25.7% (FY23/24) and 25.6% (FY24/25); FY25/26 slowed to ~13%. Post-COVID four-year average growth was 34.1% vs 5.9% pre-pandemic (NGB). Turnover growth also slowed from +30.7% to ~+17%.

**Betting is the market: R51.97bn (~$3.13bn) GGR in FY24/25, 69.8% of the total and +44.7% YoY.** Bookmaker sports/'other contingencies' alone was R47.89bn (~$2.89bn, +49.3%); bookmaker horse racing R3.52bn (~$212m, +12.3%); totalisators (4Racing, Gold Circle) R0.57bn and shrinking ~10% a year.

**Online penetration: 86% of betting GGR and ~60% of all gambling GGR is online (NGB estimate; R44.46bn/~$2.68bn disclosed by six provinces).** SARB's March 2026 Quarterly Bulletin independently reports online betting GGR of R44bn vs R29bn a year earlier (85.5% of betting revenue), corroborating the NGB figure. Because Gauteng, KZN and Free State do not disaggregate, the true online share is higher than 60%.

**Land-based is in structural decline.** Casino GGR fell 4.1% to R16.65bn (~$1.00bn, 22.3% share; 36 of a maximum 41 casinos operating after Mayfair closed in Jan 2025); bingo −8.6% to R1.73bn (~$104m); LPMs flat at R4.15bn (~$250m). Casino share of GGR has collapsed from 81.9% in FY10/11 to 22.2%.

**Geography follows licences, not population: Western Cape (R23.1bn/~$1.39bn, 31%) and Mpumalanga (R22.2bn/~$1.34bn, 30%) now out-earn Gauteng (R13.5bn/~$0.81bn, 18%)** because national-reach online bookmakers are licensed there. Mpumalanga books 54% of all betting turnover (R609bn/~$36.7bn) at a 3.5% hold; Gauteng's betting hold is 15% — a retail/horse-racing profile.

**Licensing is provincial and concurrent (Constitution Sched. 4A; National Gambling Act 7 of 2004).** Nine Provincial Licensing Authorities issue casino, bookmaker, totalisator, route/LPM and bingo licences; the NGB oversees norms, the national register of excluded persons and statistics. 315 bookmakers, 553 bookmaker outlets, 325 tote outlets, 2,546 LPM site operators (15,743 machines) and 73 bingo halls (13,452 EBTs) were operational at 31 Mar 2025. Bookmaker licence caps: Gauteng 131, KZN 48, Northern Cape 19; elsewhere unlimited 'subject to market demand'.

**Online casino ('interactive gambling') remains illegal under s11 NGA; only online betting via a provincially licensed bookmaker is lawful.** The 2008 Amendment Act that would have created national interactive licences was never proclaimed; the National Gambling Amendment Bill (B27-2018) is still in the NCOP process and the private-member Remote Gambling Bill (B11-2024) is stalled. In practice, bookmakers in WC/MP/LP offer casino-style 'fixed-odds' content (numbers, virtuals, crash games), which is the legal grey zone driving the numbers.

**Tax regime today: provincial GGR taxes plus 15% VAT on GGR plus 27% CIT.** Gauteng (GN 570/1997): casino 9%, bingo 12%, route/LPM 15%, totalisator 9% + 8.5% SDF levy, bookmakers 6.5% + 1% SDF levy. Western Cape: casinos 8–19% progressive, LPM 10–20%, bingo 10–15%, tote 6%, bookmakers 3% tax + 3% levy on winning bets. Industry (SABA) says online bookmakers 'typically' pay 6.5% of GGR; with VAT the effective burden is ~18–19% of GGR.

**Tax take: R5.81bn (~$350m) in FY24/25 (+20.1%), i.e. 7.8% of GGR; R6.44bn (~$388m) in FY25/26 (+10.8%, 7.6%).** Betting delivered 58.9% (R3.42bn/~$206m, effective 6.6%), casinos 29.5% (R1.72bn/~$103m, 10.3%), LPMs 9.0% (12.7%), bingo 2.5% (8.4%). Provinces depend on this: own-revenue is only ~3% of provincial budgets (Treasury).

**The big swing factor: National Treasury's proposed 20% national tax on online betting and interactive GGR (discussion paper, Nov 2025).** It would sit on top of provincial taxes, be administered by SARS, apply even to unlawful interactive revenue, and raise 'over R10bn' (~$0.6bn). Comments closed Feb 2026; the Minister told Parliament in the 21 Oct 2026 MTBPS that the final design comes in the Feb 2027 Budget, then a Money Bill. Combined burden would be 26–29% before VAT, ~38–40% with VAT (SABA, Whitesmans, Lurie Inc).

**Operator landscape: a dozen scaled bookmakers, three casino groups.** Hollywoodbets is widely regarded as the #1 online bookmaker [share unverified — NGB publishes no operator shares]; Betway (Super Group: Africa segment revenue $262m in Q3-26, +17%, 34% EBITDA margin — not SA-only), Supabets, Lottostar, World Sports Betting, Gbets, Playabets, Sportingbet, Easybet, Goldrush and SunBet (Sun International) are the other scaled brands. Casinos: Sun International, Tsogo Sun, Peermont. The National Lottery (Lotteries Act; NLC) sits outside NGB statistics.

**Payments are bank-rail, not mobile-money.** Instant EFT (Ozow, Capitec Pay, Stitch/SiD), debit cards and cash vouchers (1Voucher, OTT) dominate deposits; credit-card gambling is widely blocked by banks and exchange control forbids cards/forex for offshore gambling (Treasury). Gambling licensees are FICA 'accountable institutions' (KYC/AML). Minimum deposits of R10–R50 (secondary sources) underpin mass-market reach.

**Participation is the highest in the world: 32.3% of South African internet users aged 16+ visited a gambling site/app in the past month (GWI Digital 2026, #1 of 48 markets; UK 19.6%, US 10.2%).** Betting is 1.6% of the CPI basket, the 12th-largest weight (Treasury/StatsSA).

**Responsible gambling and advertising are tightening.** Industry contributed R57.4m (~$3.5m) to the National Responsible Gambling Foundation in FY25/26; the NRGF counselling line took 83,541 calls (5,443 treatment-related; 3,541 people treated). The dtic promised advertising 'norms and standards' and regulations before July 2026 [publication not verified]; the ARB consulted on a tougher Gambling Code (comments 28 Feb 2026) and signed an enforcement MoU with the NGB in Sept 2026.

**Enforcement is escalating against offshore/illegal online casino.** Government 'declared war' on illegal online gambling (Jul 2026); the NGB issued an EOI (30 Jun 2026, extended to 4 Sep 2026) for a provider to monitor and IP-block illegal sites; s16 NGA lets banks confiscate illegal winnings to the NGB. Illegal online gambling is said to drain >R50bn (~$3bn) a year (ITWeb/CNBC Africa) — basis unverified.

**Employment and transformation: 33,169 direct jobs (−3% YoY) in FY24/25; FY25/26 casinos 13,328, bookmakers 12,230.** B-BBEE is measured on the generic scorecard (casino operators average Level 1.7, LPM 2.4, bingo 3.1); provincial boards weigh empowerment in licence awards.

**Read-through for B2Tech: enter via a provincial bookmaker licence (WC or MP are the proven national-reach hubs), build on 'fixed-odds' content and instant-EFT rails, and underwrite the business at a 38–40% effective GGR tax.** A 20% national tax plus advertising limits would compress promo-led growth and favour scale incumbents with retail estates and low CAC; it also raises the odds that the eventual national interactive regime arrives with a high tax attached rather than as a liberalisation.

segments.name: Sports betting & online bookmaking
segments.headline: R52bn (~$3.1bn) and 70% of GGR; 86% online, concentrated in Western Cape and Mpumalanga licences; the whole market's growth and the whole of Treasury's target.
narrative: Betting on horse racing, sport and 'other contingencies' generated R51.97bn (~$3.13bn) of GGR in the audited year to 31 March 2025, up 44.7% on R35.91bn, and was the only mode to grow. Within it, bookmaker sports betting was R47.89bn (~$2.89bn, +49.3%), continuing a run of 57%, 61%, 55% and 49% annual growth since FY2021/22; bookmaker horse racing added R3.52bn (~$212m, +12.3%); and the totalisators (4Racing in eight provinces, Gold Circle in KZN) shrank again to R0.57bn (~$34m). Betting turnover was R1,125.6bn (~$67.8bn), 75% of all stakes, implying a blended hold of just 4.6% — and 4.3% on bookmaker sports — which is far below a conventional sportsbook margin and signals that the volume is dominated by high-frequency, high-recycling products (numbers/lottery betting, virtuals and crash-style 'fixed-odds' games) rather than match betting. Quarterly GGR ran R11.6bn, R12.1bn, R14.6bn and R13.7bn through FY24/25, so Q4 was already decelerating to +41% YoY from +50% in Q3; the NGB's FY25/26 annual report shows total market GGR growth slowing to 13.4%, and since land-based was 'relatively flat', betting growth in FY25/26 was likely in the mid-to-high teens [estimate].

The channel split is the key regulatory fact. Six provinces (WC, MP, LP, NW, EC, NC) disaggregate online from retail, and their online betting GGR was R44.46bn (~$2.68bn), 86% of all betting GGR and 59.7% of total gambling GGR; the Reserve Bank's March 2026 Quarterly Bulletin independently puts online betting at R44bn vs R29bn a year earlier (85.5% of betting revenue), so the two primary sources agree. Gauteng, KZN and Free State do not split their data and are booked as retail, so the NGB's '60% of all gambling is online' is a floor. Geography is a function of where national-reach online licences sit: Mpumalanga booked R21.33bn (41%) of betting GGR on R609bn of turnover (3.5% hold) and Western Cape R19.52bn (37%) on R343bn (5.7%), while Gauteng, with the most bookmakers (140), took only R4.66bn (9%) at a 15% hold — a retail and horse-racing profile. Betting taxes/levies were R3.42bn (~$206m), 59% of all gambling tax, at an effective 6.6% of GGR; Mpumalanga (41%) and the Western Cape (36%) collected the bulk, which is why those provinces have been content to host a 'provincial licence, national customer' model.

Supply is consolidating even as revenue grows: operational bookmakers fell from 349 to 315 (−7.1%) while outlets held at roughly 550–600 and totalisator outlets at 325, and bookmaking employment slipped from 12,899 to 12,230 in FY25/26. The NGB does not publish operator shares; Hollywoodbets is generally regarded as the largest brand, with Betway (Super Group), Supabets, Lottostar, World Sports Betting, Gbets, Playabets, Sportingbet, Easybet, Goldrush and SunBet the other scaled names [shares unverified]. Super Group's Africa segment — of which South Africa is the anchor but not the whole — grew revenue 17% to $262m in Q3-26 with a 34% adjusted EBITDA margin and $839m (+29%) over nine months, which is the best public proxy for the unit economics an incumbent is achieving here. Market behaviour is promo-heavy (sign-up bonuses, free bets, wagering requirements), which is exactly where a 20% national tax would bite first.

For an entrant the commercial logic is a bookmaker licence in a province that permits broad 'fixed-odds' content and online acceptance (Western Cape or Mpumalanga in practice), a content stack weighted to numbers, virtuals and live 'bet-games' plus a conventional sportsbook, and instant-EFT/voucher cashiering to reach a mass market that stakes small amounts frequently. The counter-case is equally clear: the product mix sits in a legal grey zone that both the dtic and Treasury describe as 'interactive gambling remains illegal'; Treasury explicitly wants to end provinces competing on headline tax to attract registrations; and advertising restrictions are coming. Underwrite the plan at a 38–40% effective GGR tax, assume promotional intensity falls, and treat the WC/MP hold rates as the realistic margin ceiling.

segments.name: Land-based: casinos, LPMs & bingo
segments.headline: R22.5bn (~$1.36bn) of GGR shrinking 3–4% a year; a capped, high-tax, high-RTP estate that still supplies 41% of provincial gambling tax.
narrative: Casinos generated R16.65bn (~$1.00bn) of GGR in FY2024/25, down 4.1% after a flat FY2023/24, on turnover of R292.8bn (~$17.6bn, −1.5%); every quarter was below the prior-year quarter (Q4 R4.01bn vs R4.31bn). Thirty-six of a maximum 41 licensed casinos were operating at 31 March 2025 after Mayfair (Eastern Cape) closed in January 2025, with 21,370 slots and 890 tables; Gauteng hosts seven casinos, 8,226 slots and 45% of casino GGR (R7.49bn/~$451m), followed by KZN (R3.55bn, 21%) and the Western Cape (R2.70bn, 16%). Average return-to-player is 94% (North West 87–88%). Casino taxes were R1.72bn (~$103m), an effective 10.3% of GGR, reflecting Gauteng's 9% flat rate and the Western Cape's 8–19% progressive scale. The NGB's FY25/26 report describes casino, bingo and LPM revenue as 'relatively flat', and casino headcount fell from 13,759 to 13,328. Sun International, Tsogo Sun and Peermont own the bulk of the estate; the NGB does not publish operator shares.

Limited payout machines — route-operated slots in bars, taverns and bingo halls, capped at five per site with low stakes/prizes — are the most resilient land-based product: R4.15bn (~$250m) of GGR (−0.04%) on R54.7bn of turnover across 2,546 site operators and 15,743 active machines, taxed at an effective 12.7% (R525m/~$32m; Gauteng's route-operator rate is 15%). Western Cape (22%) and KZN (21%) lead. Route-operator licences are capped at two in Eastern Cape, five in Gauteng and two each in Northern and Western Cape, which makes incumbents' positions (e.g., Vukani/Galaxy, Goldrush) effectively entrenched.

Bingo is a six-province (GP, KZN, MP, LP, NW, EC) electronic-bingo-terminal business: 73 outlets and 13,452 EBTs produced R1.73bn (~$104m) of GGR, down 8.6%, with taxes of R146m (~$8.8m, 8.4% effective; 12% headline in Gauteng). Western Cape, Free State and Northern Cape have 'no roll-out currently', and Gauteng caps bingo at 11 licences. Totalisator horse racing, the historic core of South African betting, has declined every year since FY2018/19 and is now R337m (~$20m).

For an operator the land-based estate matters in three ways rather than as a growth vehicle: retail outlets and casino floors remain the cheapest customer-acquisition channel for an online brand (and will matter more if advertising is curbed); casino licences carry provincial socio-economic obligations and B-BBEE scrutiny (casino operators average Level 1.7) that set the political benchmark against which 'few local benefits' online operators are judged — Treasury makes this contrast explicitly when justifying a higher online rate; and casino groups are the natural partners or acquirers for any entrant needing a provincial licence and a local balance sheet.

segments.name: Licensing & legal framework
segments.headline: A 2004 statute, nine provincial regulators, an unproclaimed 2008 online law and two stalled bills: lawful online = betting via a provincial bookmaker licence; interactive casino = illegal.
narrative: Gambling (excluding lotteries and sports pools) is a concurrent national–provincial competence under Schedule 4 Part A of the Constitution. The National Gambling Act 7 of 2004 (NGA) sets uniform norms and standards, creates the National Gambling Board (NGB) under the Department of Trade, Industry and Competition (dtic) and recognises nine Provincial Licensing Authorities (Eastern Cape Gambling Board, Free State Gambling and Liquor Authority, Gauteng Gambling Board, KZN Gaming and Betting Board, Limpopo Gambling Board, Mpumalanga Economic Regulator, Northern Cape, North West and Western Cape Gambling and Racing Boards), each with exclusive jurisdiction to license casinos, bookmakers, totalisators, route/LPM operators and bingo under its own provincial Act. The NGB keeps the national register of excluded persons, monitors market conduct and statistics, and leads illegal-gambling enforcement; the National Lottery is separately regulated by the National Lotteries Commission under the Lotteries Act 1997 (operator licence transitioned from Ithuba to Sizekhaya Holdings in 2025/26 [secondary]).

Section 11 of the NGA prohibits making an 'interactive game' available — a gambling game played over the internet other than one accessible only on licensed premises — which the dtic, NGB and Treasury all read as a ban on online casino. The National Gambling Amendment Act 10 of 2008 would have created NGB-issued national interactive licences but was never proclaimed by the President and has no legal effect. The National Gambling Amendment Bill (B27-2018), which would replace the NGB with a National Gambling Regulator and tighten enforcement, passed the National Assembly in 2018 and was still in the NCOP mandate process in late 2025, with public participation mooted for February 2026 [status as of Nov 2026 unverified]. The private-member Remote Gambling Bill (B11-2024), which proposed a national remote-gambling licence covering casino games, lapsed with the sixth Parliament and has not progressed. Online betting — bets on sport, horse racing or 'other contingencies' placed with a provincially licensed bookmaker — is lawful, and provinces such as the Western Cape, Mpumalanga and Limpopo have licensed bookmakers to accept online bets nationally and to offer fixed-odds products on numbers, virtual events and live games. This is the grey zone: legally 'betting', economically 'gaming'.

Licence supply is capped by product and province. Casinos are limited to 41 nationally (EC 5, FS 4, GP 7, KZN 5, LP 3, MP 4, NW 4+1 pending, NC 3, WC 5); route-operator licences to 2 (EC), 5 (GP), 2 (NC) and 2 (WC) with no cap elsewhere; bookmaker licences to 131 in Gauteng, 48 in KZN and 19 in the Northern Cape but unlimited (subject to market demand and viability) in the other provinces; totalisators to one per province except KZN (two); bingo to 15 (EC) and 11 (GP), with no roll-out in WC, FS and NC. Licences are granted after probity, financial, B-BBEE and socio-economic review, with public objection periods; provincial licence fees and the NGB's own levies are set by provincial regulation and were not verified for this brief [n/a]. There is no national server-location rule, but exchange control (SARB) and s16 NGA effectively ring-fence payments inside the domestic banking system.

Commercially, the framework rewards early provincial licences in 'open' provinces and penalises latecomers in capped ones. An entrant should expect 6–12 months [estimate] for a bookmaker licence, a local company with meaningful black ownership to score on the generic B-BBEE scorecard, and a product line vetted by the licensing province. The strategic risk is that the eventual national online regime — whether via the 2018 Bill, a revived remote-gambling bill, or Treasury's tax instrument as a de facto regulator — is being designed in a climate of harm reduction, not liberalisation, so the interactive-casino upside should not be in a base case.

Fees not verified [n/a]; no server-location rule, but SARB exchange control and s16 NGA ring-fence payments domestically.

blocks.heading: Strategic implications
blocks.takeaway: The framework rewards early licences in 'open' provinces; interactive-casino upside should not be in a base case.
points: Expect 6–12 months [estimate] for a bookmaker licence, a local company with meaningful black ownership, and products vetted by the licensing province.
Eventual national online regime (2018 Bill, revived remote bill, or Treasury tax instrument) is being designed for harm reduction, not liberalisation.

segments.name: Tax regime & the proposed 20% national online gambling tax
segments.headline: Today ~18–19% of online GGR all-in (6.5% provincial + VAT); Treasury wants +20% on top, worth >R10bn (~$0.6bn), with the design due in the Feb 2027 Budget.
narrative: All gambling taxes are levied on gross gambling revenue (stakes less winnings) by the provinces, which keep the proceeds; this matters because provinces raise only ~3% of their budgets from own revenue and gambling is one of the few levers they control. Gauteng's regulations (GN 570 of 1997) tax casinos at 9% of GGR, bingo at 12%, route/LPM operators at 15%, totalisators at 9% plus an 8.5% Sports Development Fund levy, bookmakers at 6.5% of gross betting revenue plus a 1% levy, and horse-racing bets at 6% plus 6%. The Western Cape applies progressive scales — casinos 8% (below R14.2m) to 19% (above R71.0m), LPMs 10–20%, bingo 10–15% — a 6% totalisator rate and, for bookmakers, a 3% tax plus a 3% levy on winning bets; Treasury characterises bookmakers nationally as paying 6–7% (elsewhere 6–9%) and casinos 10–15%. KZN, Mpumalanga and Limpopo rates were not verified for this brief [n/a]. On top sit 15% VAT, which bookmakers account for on GGR (an effective 12–13% after input recovery, per SABA), 27% corporate income tax and the skills development levy; gambling winnings are not taxed in the hands of recreational punters, although habitual professional winnings are taxable income. The out-turn: R5.81bn (~$350m) of provincial gambling tax in FY24/25 (7.8% of GGR; betting 6.6%, casinos 10.3%, LPMs 12.7%, bingo 8.4%) and R6.44bn (~$388m) in FY25/26 (7.6%).

National Treasury's discussion paper 'The case for a national online gambling tax' (published Nov 2025; comments closed Feb 2026) proposes a 20% national tax on the GGR of online betting including interactive gambling, in addition to provincial taxes, collected by SARS using the same returns operators already file with provincial boards, and applying to any locally based operator's interactive revenue 'to the extent' it is earned even though interactive gambling is illegal. Treasury's stated aims are to internalise the social cost of problem gambling, to stop provinces competing on headline rates to attract registrations, and — explicitly a secondary objective — to raise 'over R10 billion' (~$0.6bn) a year, roughly 1.7x the entire current provincial gambling-tax take. The paper benchmarks 11 jurisdictions at 20% and 16 above it, cites the UK (RGD 21%, GBD 15%) and Australian POCTs (15–25%), and acknowledges Kenya's 2019–20 experience, where a 20% stake excise drove operators and punters offshore and was repealed.

Industry arithmetic (SABA, Whitesmans Attorneys, Lurie Inc/SAROGA) puts the combined rate at 26.5% of GGR before VAT and 38–40% all-in, versus Treasury's own 26–29% pre-VAT figure, and warns of migration to unlicensed offshore sites, provincial revenue erosion and job losses; a constitutional challenge is also flagged, since a national tax on a provincially licensed, provincially taxed activity must proceed as a s77 Money Bill. Finance Minister Godongwana's 21 October 2026 MTBPS confirmed consultations are ongoing on 'the tax design, its linkages to the existing regulatory framework, and the implications for provinces and the currently regulated market', with the final design to be announced in the February 2027 Budget, followed by legislation — so the earliest realistic effective date is FY2027/28 [estimate].

The commercial implication for an operator is that a pure-online model priced for an 18–19% effective GGR tax would see roughly a fifth of gross margin removed at a stroke; at Betway-type Africa EBITDA margins of ~34% the hit is survivable for scale players but would likely be passed through as lower bonuses, tighter odds and higher wagering requirements, and would trim the ~4–6% hold products hardest. Smaller licensees, which are already exiting (315 bookmakers from 349), would consolidate. The upside scenario is that Treasury lands at a lower rate (10–15%) or offsets VAT; the downside is a 20% rate plus a VAT-inclusive base. Any entry model should be stress-tested at the 38–40% all-in level and assume that provincial headline competition — the arbitrage that made WC and MP the hubs — disappears.

segments.name: Payments, responsible gambling, advertising & enforcement
segments.headline: Bank-rail payments and world-leading participation meet a 2026 tightening cycle: advertising norms, an NGB–ARB enforcement pact and an IP-blocking programme against offshore casino.
narrative: South Africa's cashier stack is domestic bank rails rather than mobile money: instant EFT via Ozow, Capitec Pay and Stitch/SiD, Visa/Mastercard debit cards, and cash-bought vouchers (1Voucher, OTT) sold at major retail tills, with ATM and retail-counter deposits for the unbanked; secondary guides report minimum deposits of R10–R50 at the major bookmakers. Credit-card gambling is widely declined by issuers, and the exchange-control regime requires Authorised Dealers to refuse foreign-currency purchases and card payments for offshore gambling, while s16 NGA obliges banks to withhold unlawful winnings and remit them to the NGB in trust pending forfeiture — a real, if patchily enforced, deterrent to offshore play. Gambling licensees are FICA accountable institutions, so KYC at registration, source-of-funds checks and suspicious-transaction reporting to the Financial Intelligence Centre are standard, and payouts must go to a verified account in the player's name.

Participation is extreme by any benchmark: GWI's Digital 2026 report ranks South Africa first of 48 markets with 32.3% of internet users aged 16+ visiting a gambling site or app in the previous month (Ghana 21.5%, UK 19.6%, Nigeria 18%, Kenya 16%, US 10.2%) — a measure of visits, not spend. Betting is 1.6% of the CPI basket, the 12th-largest weight. Statutory protections are the NGA's minimum age of 18, the ban on extending credit, the national register of excluded persons (self- and third-party exclusion administered by the NGB), mandatory problem-gambling messaging in advertising, and the industry-funded National Responsible Gambling Foundation (NRGF): R57.4m (~$3.5m) of contributions in FY25/26, 1.26m helpline contacts (mostly operational queries), 83,541 counselling-line calls, 5,443 treatment-related and 3,541 people treated. Survey reporting through 2026 (Yazi, stokvel studies) and parliamentary questions on gambling-linked suicide risk have made harm the dominant political frame.

Advertising is where the rules are moving fastest. Section 15 NGA and the 2004 regulations already prohibit targeting minors, false claims and ads without the responsible-gambling warning; in February 2026 the dtic told Parliament it would publish 'norms and standards' on gambling advertising together with advertising regulations before July 2026 [publication not verified as of 11 Nov 2026]; the Advertising Regulatory Board consulted on amendments to its Gambling Code (comments due 28 Feb 2026); and in September 2026 the NGB and ARB formalised a memorandum of understanding to jointly monitor and act on gambling advertising, with a betting operator publicly apologising in October 2026 after a promotion reached a preschool. Expect restrictions on timing, media, bonus advertising and sports-sponsorship visibility in the next 12 months rather than a UK-style whistle-to-whistle ban [view].

Enforcement is now a stated government priority. The NGB chairs an Illegal Gambling Task Team with SAPS and provincial boards, has run joint raids on illegal machines, and on 30 June 2026 issued an Expression of Interest (deadline extended to 4 September 2026) for a specialist provider to identify, monitor and block illegal gambling websites targeting South Africans, with evidence shared for prosecution under the NGA; government ministers 'declared war' on illegal online gambling in July 2026, citing estimates that unlicensed sites drain more than R50bn (~$3bn) a year from the economy — a figure whose basis is unverified and which should be read as advocacy, not measurement. For an operator the practical consequences are that offshore-licensed casino brands face rising payment and DNS friction, that licensed operators' compliance (ad content, affiliate marketing, KYC, exclusion-list checks) will be audited more actively by both the ARB and PLAs, and that the political reward for being demonstrably 'licensed and responsible' is rising just as the tax cost of that status rises too.

highlights.text: Scale and momentum: R84.5bn (~$5.1bn) GGR growing 13% even after a 26% year, with ~60%+ online — the largest regulated online betting pool in Africa and one of the deepest per-capita anywhere (32.3% monthly participation).

Lawful national-reach online betting under a single provincial bookmaker licence, with unlimited licence supply in WC/MP/LP/EC/FS and a permissive 'fixed-odds' content envelope (numbers, virtuals, live games) that monetises like casino at 6.5% provincial tax.

Mature payments and identity rails: instant EFT, Capitec Pay, vouchers and FICA-grade KYC let an operator reach banked and unbanked customers at R10–R50 tickets without mobile-money dependency or operator-borne wallet float.

Land-based decline (casino −4.1%, bingo −8.6%) is pushing incumbent casino groups toward online partnerships and selling retail-acquisition capacity cheaply — a route to licences, B-BBEE-compliant local structures and low-CAC distribution.
Consolidation among bookmakers (349 → 315 operational) and a coming tax/advertising squeeze favour scaled, well-capitalised entrants able to acquire sub-scale licensees rather than build greenfield.

Enforcement against offshore casino (IP blocking, bank withholding of winnings, ARB–NGB pact) raises the value of a licensed position: the >R50bn (~$3bn) 'illegal' pool, whatever its true size, is addressable only by licensees.

lowlights.text: Treasury's proposed 20% national tax on online GGR would lift the all-in burden from ~18–19% to 38–40%; final design in the Feb 2027 Budget, likely effective FY2027/28 [estimate]. Promo-led growth and 4–6% hold products are most exposed.

Interactive casino remains illegal (NGA s11; 2008 Act unproclaimed; B27-2018 and B11-2024 stalled): the casino-style 'fixed-odds' content underpinning WC/MP revenue sits in a grey zone that a national regulator or SARS could re-characterise.

Advertising restrictions (dtic norms and standards, ARB Gambling Code, NGB–ARB MoU) are arriving in a harm-dominated political climate; expect limits on bonus advertising, timing and sports visibility that raise CAC for new brands.

Growth is decelerating (GGR +25.6% → +13.4%; turnover +30.7% → ~+17%) and the NRGF/survey evidence of harm (5,443 treatment-related calls; stokvel and grocery-money studies) gives regulators cover for stake, deposit or product limits.

Provincial fragmentation: nine regulators, differing tax bases (GP 6.5%+1%; WC 3%+3% on winning bets), caps on bookmaker licences in GP/KZN/NC and unverified licence fees; Treasury explicitly intends to end inter-provincial rate competition.

Data quality: Gauteng's FY25/26 numbers are provisional; three provinces do not split online/retail; the NGB's own text contradicts its tables on outlet counts and casino shares — model on audited FY24/25 figures and treat FY25/26 as indicative.

Macro and FX: a rand at ~16.6/USD, 15% VAT and weak consumer incomes mean USD-reported returns are volatile and the political optics of R1.76tn 'wagered' (turnover, not spend — as SARB itself cautioned) keep the sector a fiscal target.

forecast.intro: The regulatory 'bridge' from the audited FY2024/25 base to today runs through four moving parts. The NGB's 2025/26 Annual Report (tabled Oct 2026) lifts the market from R74.5bn (~$4.49bn) to R84.46bn (~$5.09bn) GGR and provincial taxes from R5.81bn to R6.44bn (~$388m), with growth slowing from 26% to 13% and still entirely online-betting-led. Against that base, National Treasury's 20% national tax on online and interactive GGR (worth >R10bn/~$0.6bn) moved from discussion paper (Nov 2025) through consultation (closed Feb 2026) to a confirmed design announcement in the February 2027 Budget (MTBPS, 21 Oct 2026). In parallel the dtic promised advertising norms and standards (by Jul 2026; publication unverified), the NGB tendered for site-blocking (EOI Jun–Sep 2026) and signed an enforcement MoU with the ARB (Sep 2026), while the structural fix — a national interactive-gambling licence via the 2018 Amendment Bill or a remote-gambling bill — has not advanced.
forecast.view: Our base case is that **the market reaches ~R92–95bn (~$5.5–5.7bn) GGR in FY2026/27 (+9–12%) [estimate]**, with betting passing 72% of GGR and online passing 65%, as sports-betting growth normalises toward the mid-teens and land-based drifts 2–4% lower; **provincial tax take rises to ~R7.0bn (~$420m) [estimate]**. On tax, we expect Treasury to **confirm a national online GGR tax in February 2027 but at a rate and base softened from the paper — most likely 10–15% with transitional relief or VAT interaction addressed — effective no earlier than FY2027/28 [view]**; a straight 20% on top of VAT would, on Treasury's own Kenya analysis, push volume offshore and cut the provincial base it needs. The legislative response (B27-2018 or a successor) is more likely to be reshaped around the tax than to legalise interactive casino within two years. **Advertising rules will tighten first** (bonus/inducement advertising, time-of-day, sports kit), raising CAC and favouring brands with retail estates. Operator margins in the online segment, currently supported by ~34% regional EBITDA margins at the leader, should compress by roughly 10–15 points under a 20% scenario and 5–8 points under a 10–15% scenario [estimate], driving further consolidation among the 315 licensed bookmakers. Leverage in the sector is low and self-funded; the risk is regulatory, not balance-sheet. Swing factors: the February 2027 rate; whether SARS or the provinces administer it; the published scope of 'interactive' revenue; the dtic advertising regulations; and the NGB blocking programme's effectiveness against offshore casino.
watch: February 2027 Budget: headline rate, base (online betting only vs all 'interactive'), VAT treatment, revenue-sharing with provinces and effective date of the national online gambling tax.

Publication of dtic gambling-advertising norms and standards and regulations (promised before July 2026) and the first ARB/NGB joint rulings under the Sept 2026 MoU — scope for bonus and sports-sponsorship limits.
NCOP progress on the National Gambling Amendment Bill (B27-2018) and any revived remote-gambling bill; whether a National Gambling Regulator assumes licensing of online activity.
NGB appointment of the illegal-website monitoring/blocking provider (EOI closed 4 Sep 2026) and first blocking orders; bank-side enforcement of s16 withholding.
NGB FY2025/26 audited statistics (due ~Oct 2026/early 2027) and Q1–Q2 FY2026/27 quarterlies: online share by province, bookmaker count, and whether Gauteng's provisional numbers are revised.

Provincial responses: Western Cape and Mpumalanga rate or licence-condition changes to defend their R19–21bn betting bases; any province moving to disaggregate online data or to cap bookmaker licences.
Operator signals: Super Group Africa margins and Hollywoodbets/Sun International disclosures on promo intensity, retail footprint and any M&A among sub-scale licensees.
